title: Turning an eight-hour database update into minutes
question: Tell me about a performance problem you solved.

situation: The system relied on a legacy Soundex pipeline for processing street name data that already suffered from severe performance issues, taking up to eight hours to execute across millions of records.
task: My explicit task was simply to add a new set of prefixes and suffixes to the phonetic cleaning logic. But because the eight-hour execution time made local testing and database validation agonisingly slow, I took the initiative to optimise both the matching algorithm and the underlying database layer.
action: Proactive algorithmic refactoring: to clean street names efficiently before Soundex encoding, I implemented a prefix trie in C#. A trie makes almost no difference for a single record, but scaling it across millions eliminated redundant lookups and cut the algorithmic execution time in half.

Database optimisation: lacking direct access to the legacy querying application's source, I reverse-engineered the query execution patterns. I turned individual sequential row updates into high-throughput batched multi-update queries to write the computed Soundex values back into the target database efficiently.
result: Total processing time fell from eight hours to a few minutes, turning a painful testing bottleneck into a system-wide performance breakthrough across millions of records.

challenge: Reverse-engineering the end-to-end data flow and diagnosing the database performance bottlenecks without direct visibility into the legacy application's source code.
hardestBug: Discovering why the legacy C# process was forced to run in Debug mode. Stepping through execution uncovered a hidden off-by-one index error that caused memory boundary exceptions in Release mode. Resolving it let us compile and run optimised Release builds safely.
differently: I would build an automated comparison tool upfront to continuously validate parity between the old and new implementations. Early on I relied too heavily on testing against a local instance of the product. A standalone verification script from the start would have given immediate feedback and isolated algorithm correctness from local environment state.
aboutYourself: This project reinforced that I excel at deep technical troubleshooting, and at applying theoretical computer science to practical, high-impact business problems. It showed me that I thrive on complex, low-visibility performance challenges where I can dig into the data structures and the query mechanics.
enjoyed: Applying advanced data structures like tries to a real system bottleneck, and seeing an eight-hour process collapse into a matter of minutes.
